persona: The modern JRPG player: recently played Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, Metaphor: ReFantazio, Honkai: Star Rail and Octopath Traveler II; judges production value against those and flags anything that looks cheap, dated or cluttered.

F01.note: The dragon owns the phone screen, but the bottom sixth is dead black under three lonely buttons and the party is buried behind their own cards.

F02.note: Moody behind-the-party shot, but Kimahri vanishes behind Tidus and Seymour feels far away.

F03.note: The gilded proscenium is a bold theatrical idea, but the HUD is stacked on top of the frame and the fight shrinks to a postcard.

F04.note: The boss is crammed against the command list while my party is a tiny line far right, and the Mortiorchis tag lands on Kimahri.

F05.note: VS-screen energy with Tidus and Seymour splash panels: great as a two-second intro, exhausting as the screen I stare at every turn.

F06.note: Film-still depth with Yuna huge in the foreground and the HUD tucked into the bands, but Paine stands on the dragon's chest so the boss reads small.

F07.note: Solid, readable three-quarter line-up in a detailed corridor; the dragon hovers without touching anything.

F08.note: Dragon poster plus gacha portrait cards: crystal clear, but it looks like a mobile menu, not a battlefield.

F09.note: Classic FFX face-off made cinematic by the bands; everyone reads at a glance, though Kimahri hides behind Tidus.

F10.note: Seymour looms nicely, but the HP block sits on his robe and the menu clips Mortiorchis's blade.

F11.note: Moonlit and balanced, but the turn-order column crowds Seymour and my HP sits under the enemy.

F12.note: Huge dragon, but the three girls are welded into one tiny clump at its tail.

F13.note: Tabletop tokens on a map: perfectly legible and completely lifeless.

F14.note: Gorgeous rim-lit villain's-eye shot, but picking commands while looking at my own party from behind the boss feels backwards, and Mortiorchis is off screen.

F15.note: Star Rail-style backs to camera with a big dragon, but the right edge is a pile-up of wing, menu and HP.

F16.note: Good FFX-style diagonal with soft bokeh, but Tidus's legs disappear behind the command list.

F17.note: The three girls collapse into one blob in the middle with the dragon peeking over their heads.

F18.note: Balanced over-the-shoulder with Seymour centred and big; Kimahri is lost behind Tidus.

F19.note: Same good three-quarter staging as the sharp corridor version; the bokeh flatters the paintings but turns the arena to mush.

F20.note: Tidus front and centre with the party fanned around him reads like a modern third-person JRPG; the HUD eats both sides.

F21.note: Three heroines' backs lead the eye straight up to a big, clean, rim-lit dragon: this looks like a 2026 JRPG.

F22.note: One step closer than F21: the dragon is more imposing and its tail wraps behind Paine, still clean.

F23.note: The best phone layout: boss poster on top, party in front of him, a tidy command grid with no wasted space.

F24.note: Beautiful key-art pose, but it is a poster: no HUD, and the girls turn their backs on the dragon.

F25.note: A giant Yuna face parked on half the screen with the boss bar across her hair: a cut-in that forgot to leave.

F26.note: Moody cyan-rimmed dragon silhouette, but the whole HUD is stacked on it and the party is tiny.

F27.note: Three panels, three HUD blocks and a boss bar straddling a divider: stylish parts that do not add up to a readable fight.

F28.note: The cleanest shot here: the party fans out to frame Seymour, snow in the air, and the bands keep every HUD element off the painting.

F29.note: The prettiest image in the set, but it is a promo poster: no commands, no HP, the heroes posing for the camera instead of facing Seymour.

F30.note: Moonlit three-quarter view that feels like classic FFX, but the command list covers Tidus's legs.

F31.note: First-person boss poster: Seymour looks great, but with no party in the world it plays like a card game.

F32.note: Octopath-style side-on line-up, but everyone is small and half the screen is empty floor.

F33.note: Camera jammed into the party's backs; Tidus's head blows out to white and the HP bars sit on Yuna.

F34.note: Tidus's face fills the left half with the command list printed across his chest: loud, but not a battlefield.

F35.note: Mirroring shoves the party's backs into the HUD column; the right third is a traffic jam.

F36.note: The party is squeezed right up against the command list while the dragon floats alone on the left.

F37.note: The high tactics angle turns the party into small standees and Seymour into a floating decal.

F38.note: Tidy and cinematic, Yuna and Rikku read instantly, but the heavy blur makes the arena a photo backdrop.

F39.note: The stage frame suits a showbiz vibe, but the menu, HP and boss bar are slapped over the gilt and curtains.

F40.note: The party surrounding the dragon on a lit floor looks fresh, but nobody casts a shadow next to that hard pillar shadow.

F41.note: Nice foreground depth from Yuna, but Paine is pasted onto the dragon's chest and the menu clips a wing.

F42.note: Lovely mountain vista, but the party is tiny and Seymour is shoved into the turn-order column.

F43.note: Colossal Seymour is striking, but the party is pasted onto his robe and melts into the same blue.

F44.note: Pretty sci-fi floor with a glowing pad, but from up here it is a tactics map, not a boss fight.

F45.note: The command list sits right on top of Mortiorchis, one of the two things I am supposed to target.

F46.note: Classic party-on-the-right layout with a sharp corridor and a clear dragon, but my HUD sits under the enemy, far from my heroes.

S01.note: Proper action-camera grammar (over-the-shoulder command, side-on hit, painted reverse, worm's-eye colossus, low-angle victory): this is what makes the fight feel expensive.

S02.note: The bands hold the HUD rock-steady while the camera leans in per submenu; tasteful and calm, though the high White Magic angle adds little.

S03.note: The flower reticle is a lovely touch, but blurring Bahamut exactly when I am aiming at it is backwards.

S04.note: A slow orbit with a black pillar wipe to hide the card swap: clever, but the screen blacks out mid-menu, the party changes sides and the dragon's rear looks like a different monster.

S05.note: Snappy cuts tied to the menu (behind Tidus to aim, high for spells, close for items): readable and never floaty.

S06.note: The camera slides behind whoever's turn it is with a Paine splash cut-in: very Metaphor, as long as the cut-in stays short under ATB.

S07.note: Smooth crane and dolly moves feel premium, but racking the target out of focus while I aim at it hurts.

S08.note: The best FFX-2 menu camera: a sharp flower on Bahamut, a high shot of the trio for skills, a close push behind Paine for items.

S09.note: Whole-turn rhythm like Star Rail: behind the active hero, crane up for enemy moves, a Kimahri cut-in on the hand-off.

S10.note: Whip pans on every menu step: exciting once, nauseating by the tenth turn.

S11.note: Rock-solid static camera with the flower reticle: perfectly readable, but it feels like a menu over a still painting.

S12.note: Static master with a reticle: calm and clear, but Seymour never gets a single dramatic angle.

S13.note: The showpiece: worm's-eye Mega Flare wind-up, red-graded reverse on impact and a leaping low-angle victory.

S14.note: Whip pans smear the whole screen on every menu step, and Bahamut's hit lands inside the blur where I cannot read it.

top5.reason: Premium and readable at once: the party's backs fan out to frame Seymour, the letterbox bands carry turn order and HP so the painting stays clean; closest to Clair Obscur / Star Rail grammar.
The FFX-2 equivalent: the girls' backs lead the eye up to a big rim-lit dragon, spacing is clean and the HUD hugs the right edge; screenshot-worthy.
Same family as F21, one step closer: the dragon is more imposing and its tail wraps behind Paine for real depth; a hair busier on the right edge.
Letterboxed film still with a huge foreground Yuna: the most cinematic frame that still plays, though the dragon should be bigger and clear of Paine.
Classic FFX face-off in bands: faces visible, sides unmistakable, calm HUD; the safe, readable master shot.

bottom3.reason: Tabletop tokens: no painting, no scale, no drama; it looks like a virtual tabletop or a prototype, the opposite of eye candy.
A giant static Tidus face with the command list printed across his chest and Seymour squeezed under the turn order: cluttered and cheap-looking.
The same problem for FFX-2: half the screen is a frozen Yuna face, the boss bar cuts through her hair, and Rikku and Paine have left the fight.

topSequences.reason: The trailer in six frames: over-the-shoulder flower reticle, side-on hit, painted reverse for Bahamut's turn, worm's-eye Mega Flare wind-up with a red grade, and a leaping low-angle victory.
The same grammar for Seymour: the worm's-eye colossus and the reverse over his robe sell the scale, and the low hero angle lands the victory.
Behind the active hero, crane up for enemy moves, a cut-in on the hand-off to Kimahri: the Star Rail / Metaphor turn rhythm, as long as cut-ins stay short.

wholeGame: I would want the whole game to look like F28 for FFX and F21 for FFX-2 while I choose commands, then hand over to the S13 / S01 action camera the moment I confirm. The master is a calm, readable over-the-shoulder shot with the party framing the boss and the HUD pushed to the edges (bands for FFX); the action camera sells every hit: side-on for my attack, a painted reverse for the enemy's turn, worm's-eye for the big attack, a low hero angle for victory. That is the rhythm Star Rail, Clair Obscur and Metaphor taught me: stillness while you think, spectacle when something happens. Keep S09's behind-the-active-hero hand-off with a short cut-in; drop anything that moves the camera on every menu step (whip pans, orbits, racking the target soft), and never leave a giant face, a triptych or tokens on screen as the resting state.
